newsitem.title: FRANCE: France cutting defence budget in military reform.
newsitem.headline: France cutting defence budget in military reform.

text.p: France will reduce its defence budget by 2.4 percent in 1997, the first year in a five-year period leading to the establishment of all-professional armed forces, Defence Minister Charles Millon has said.

Transcripts of his statement to the Senate (upper house of parliament) released on Friday showed he announced a defence budget of 190.9 billion francs ($36.7 billion), down from 195.6 billion francs ($37.6 billion) this year.
President Jacques Chirac has launched an overhaul of the country's military that will gradually abolish conscription and cut the forces to a staff of about 350,000 from half a million by 2002.

Millon denied recent press reports that the reform would seriously curtail France's capacity for long-range action until 2000. He told the Senate the transition would only slightly affect the capacity to send forces abroad.
But he forecast the cost of operations abroad in 1997 at 2.5 billion francs ($480 million), down from expenses of 4.1 billion francs ($788.4 million) this year.
Chirac, who took power in May 1995, pushed through his modernisation plan precisely to increase the military's capacity for long-term actions overseas.

Press reports have said army chiefs reported that France would be unable to field more than 20,000 men at a time for overseas action, ruling out participation in a Gulf War scenario. France now has forces in Africa and the IFOR peace implementation force in Bosnia.
Millon announced that the armed forces staff, including civilian employees, would be reduce by around 70,000 to 504,500 next year.
About 1,000 officers and 10,500 non-commissioned officers will be given financial incentives to take early retirement or to take six-month leave to prepare for conversion to civilian jobs.
